summary: AstraHealth is mission-control software for the human body during long-duration spaceflight. It gathers astronaut-entered and simulated habitat/suit readings across physical, mental, and social health; turns them into an explainable readiness score; and shows which body systems are driving the change through an interactive 3D anatomy view. A two-minute Systems Check combines automatic vitals and sleep capture with subjective context, then produces a Systems Report with the top factors and a concrete next action. Training plans, a privacy-aware crew layer, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 screens, and a Mission Log with points, ranks, streaks, and achievements help astronauts stay consistent without tying rewards to health values. An Earth-side Flight Surgeon console adds early warning, clinical notes, alert review, and Flight Surgeon SI decision support, with red-flag escalation and explicit “guidance, not diagnosis” language. Reference ranges, countermeasures, and citations are grounded in NASA Human Research Program material. AstraHealth addresses NASA’s challenge by helping astronauts recognize, understand, and act on health risks when the nearest flight surgeon is far away.
details:
AstraHealth — mission-control software for the human body

What it does and how it works

AstraHealth is a browser-based health-monitoring and decision-support system for astronauts on long-duration missions. It combines automatic simulated habitat and suit readings with astronaut-entered context, then turns them into an explainable readiness score instead of a single opaque number.

The system has two connected experiences:

- Astronaut Flight Deck — a daily readiness view built from six physiological domains. It shows the strongest contributing factors, a 30-day mission tape, active alerts, a seven-day trend, and an interactive 3D body view with skin, muscle, and skeleton layers. Selecting a body system reveals its score, readings, reference range, and trend.

- Flight Surgeon console — an Earth-side workspace where the medical officer chooses an astronaut and reviews the same record through overview, body, trends, captures, quizzes and screens, clinical notes, and Copilot. It adds a 48–72-hour early-warning view, alert acknowledgement, clinical assessments, and check-in or measurement requests sent back to the crew.

The daily Systems Check is a short wizard. Vitals, load, and sleep arrive automatically from simulated sensors; the astronaut adds mood, stress, symptoms, hydration, and nutrition. Submitting produces a Systems Report with the score change, top factors, active alerts, and a recommended next action. Sleep and vitals are pre-filled and locked until the astronaut deliberately overrides them.

Readiness uses a 21-day personal baseline, z-scores, domain weights, a data-coverage gate, and hard rules that never wait for a trend. Every score exposes its factors. If there is not enough data, the app says so rather than inventing reassurance.

The loop continues through training plans, countermeasure links, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 mental-health screens, a privacy-aware crew layer, and a Mission Log with mission points, rank, streaks, and 17 achievements. Points reward consistency, never health readings.

Benefits and intended impact

AstraHealth is designed for the moment when the nearest flight surgeon is minutes or hours away. It helps astronauts:

- notice a meaningful change early;

- understand why the score changed;

- know the next action, not just the number;

- escalate red flags quickly;

- keep physical, mental, and social health in one record;

- stay consistent without turning health into a competition.

For the flight surgeon, it provides a compact, shared record, early-warning signals, cited context, and a way to send focused follow-ups. The intended impact is earlier intervention, better crew–ground communication, and more autonomy on long missions — while keeping clinical judgment with the flight surgeon.

Tools and technology

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS v4, TanStack Query, React Router, Motion, Recharts, Three.js, MediaPipe Tasks Vision, Workbox, IndexedDB.

- Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy 2, Alembic, PostgreSQL 16, psycopg, PyJWT, Argon2, Pytest.

- Data and content: NASA Human Research Program and Human Research Roadmap material, NASA DONKI space-weather context, NASA OSDR references, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 instruments.

- 3D and visual assets: Z-Anatomy and BodyParts3D anatomy models, Draco compression, Geist typography, Lucide icons.

- Infrastructure: Vercel for the frontend and serverless API, Neon Postgres, Docker/Podman for local deployment, Playwright, axe-core, and Lighthouse for verification.

- Hardware: no custom hardware is required. The app runs in a standard browser; the camera pulse check is optional, and habitat/suit captures are clearly labeled simulated data.

What makes it creative

The creativity is in the combination: a 3D anatomical health view, a dual astronaut/surgeon product, a mission-tape timeline, and a motivation loop that never ranks health values. The interface is deliberately calm and low-density — closer to a flight deck than a hospital dashboard — with detail revealed only when the user asks for it. The strongest idea is the closed loop: a reading becomes an explanation, an explanation becomes an action, and the action becomes part of the mission record.

Factors the team considered

- Safety: guidance, not diagnosis; red-flag escalation; rule-based refusals; a human flight surgeon remains responsible for clinical decisions.

- Trust: every score exposes factors, baselines, and citations; sparse data is labeled insufficient.

- Privacy: consent-based crew sharing and no health values in rankings.

- Usability under stress: short check-ins, large visual states, progressive disclosure, keyboard access, and reduced-motion support.

- Mission reality: comms delay, offline drafts, sync-on-reconnect, and a clear distinction between real input and simulated telemetry.

- Honesty: simulated crew and sensor data are labeled; the readiness model is a transparent heuristic, not a validated medical device.

- Maintainability: typed API contracts, migrations, tests, smoke checks, and a documented design system.

AstraHealth is a working prototype. It is not clinically validated and does not replace a flight surgeon, but it demonstrates how an astronaut-facing health system can be explainable, actionable, and calm under mission constraints.
